11 compensation for time spent responding to the Data Breach and other types of harm, free credit

12 monitoring and identity theft insurance, and injunctive relief including substantial improvements to

13 Defendant’s data security policies and practices.

 4      A. Background on Defendant

 5          11.    Defendant is a privately owned American communication and social media platform

 6 and accumulates highly private PII of its customers, which is used to engage in its business.

 7          12.    Due to the nature of the services it provides, Defendant acquires and electronically

 8 stores PII. Defendant was therefore required to ensure that PII was not disclosed or disseminated to
 9 unauthorized third parties without Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ express written consent.

10 Defendant’s duty to adopt reasonable measures to protect the PII of Plaintiff and Class Members from

11 involuntary disclosure to third parties, including in selecting its vendors, encrypting the information,

12 and purging information of past customers.

13          13.    Upon information and belief, Defendant made promises and representations to its
14 customers that PII collected from them, including that of Plaintiff and Class Members, would be kept

15 save and confidential, that the privacy of that information would be maintained, and that Defendant

16 would delete any sensitive information after it was no longer required to maintain it.

17      B. The Data Breach
18          14.     On or about October 3, 2025, Defendant posted on its website notice of breach letters

19 (“Notice Letter”). The Notice Letter states:

21          At Discord, protecting the privacy and security of our users is a top priority. That’s why
22          it’s important to us that we’re transparent with them about events that impact their
            personal information.
23
            Recently, we discovered an incident where an unauthorized party compromised one of
24          Discord’s third-party customer service providers. The unauthorized party then gained
            access to information from a limited number of users who had contacted Discord
25
            through our Customer Support and/or Trust & Safety teams.
26
            As soon as we became aware of this attack, we took immediate steps to address the
27          situation. This included revoking the customer support provider’s access to our
            ticketing system, launching an internal investigation, engaging a leading computer

24

14         E. Defendant Acquires, Collects, and Stores Individuals’ PII
15              24.     As a condition of obtaining services from Defendant, Plaintiff and Class Members were
16 required to give their sensitive and confidential PII to Defendant.

20              26.     By obtaining, collecting, and storing the PII of Plaintiff and Class Members, Defendant

21 assumed legal and equitable duties and knew or should have known that they were responsible for

22 protecting the PII from disclosure.

 4           29.     In April 2020, ZDNet reported in an article titled “Ransomware mentioned in 1,000+

11 ransomware tactics over time to include pressuring victims for payment by threatening to release

12 stolen data if they refuse to pay and publicly naming and shaming victims as secondary forms of

13 extortion.” 7

14           31.     Stolen PII is often trafficked on the dark web, as is the case here. Law enforcement has

15 difficulty policing the dark web due to this encryption, which allows users and criminals to conceal

16 identities and online activity.

17           32.     When malicious actors infiltrate companies and copy and exfiltrate the PII that those

18 companies store, that stolen information often ends up on the dark web because the malicious actors

19 buy and sell that information for profit. 8

21 AlphaBay in 2017, AlphaBay had more than 350,000 listings, many of which concerned stolen or

22 fraudulent documents that could be used to assume another person’s identity. Other marketplaces,

23 similar to the now-defunct AlphaBay, “are awash with [PII] belonging to victims from countries all

24 over the world. One of the key challenges of protecting PII online is its pervasiveness. As data breaches

25 in the news continue to show, PII about employees, customers and the public is housed in all kinds of

13        G. Defendant Failed to Comply with FTC Guidelines
14           42.      According to the Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”), the need for data security should
15 be factored into all business decision-making. To that end, the FTC has issued numerous guidelines

16 identifying best data security practices that businesses, such as Defendant, should employ to protect

17 against the unlawful exposure of PII/PHI.

18           43.      In 2016, the FTC updated its publication, Protecting Personal Information: A Guide for

19 Business, which established guidelines for fundamental data security principles and practices for

20 business. The guidelines explain that businesses should: (i) protect the personal customer information

21 that they keep; (ii) properly dispose of personal information that is no longer needed; (iii) encrypt

22 information stored on computer networks; (iv) understand their network’s vulnerabilities; and (v)

23 implement policies to correct security problems.

15      I. The Data Breach Caused Injury to Class Members and Will Result in Additional Harm
16          Such as Fraud.
17          54.     Without detailed disclosure to the victims of the Data Breach, individuals whose PII
18 was compromised by the Data Breach, including Plaintiff and Class Members, were unknowingly and

19 unwittingly exposed to continued misuse and ongoing risk of misuse of their PII for months without

20 being able to take available precautions to prevent imminent harm.

21          55.     The ramifications of Defendant’s failure to secure Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ data

22 are severe.

23          56.     Victims of data breaches are much more likely to become victims of identity theft and

24 other types of fraudulent schemes. This conclusion is based on an analysis of four years of data that

25 correlated each year’s data breach victims with those who also reported being victims of identity fraud.

26          57.     The FTC defines identity theft as “a fraud committed or attempted using the identifying

 1 information of another person without authority.” 16 The FTC describes “identifying information” as

 2 “any name or number that may be used, alone or in conjunction with any other information, to identify

 3 a specific person.” 17

 4            58.      Identity thieves can use PII, such as that of Plaintiff and Class Members, which

 5 Defendant failed to keep secure, to perpetrate a variety of crimes that harm victims. For instance,

 6 identity thieves may commit various types of government fraud such as: immigration fraud; obtaining

 7 a driver’s license or identification card in the victim’s name but with another’s picture; using the

 8 victim’s information to obtain government benefits; or filing a fraudulent tax return using the victim’s
 9 information to obtain a fraudulent refund.

10            59.      As demonstrated herein, these and other instances of fraudulent misuse of the
11 compromised PII has already occurred and are likely to continue.

12            60.      Reimbursing a consumer for a financial loss due to fraud does not make that individual
13 whole again. On the contrary, identity theft victims must spend numerous hours and their own money

14 repairing the impact to their credit. After conducting a study, the Department of Justice’s Bureau of

15 Justice Statistics (“BJS”) found that identity theft victims “reported spending an average of about 7

16 hours clearing up the issues” and resolving the consequences of fraud in 2014. 18
